description: AION SPACE is a team of five friends studying mechatronics engineering at the National University of Engineering (UNI) in Lima, Peru, united by curiosity and a passion for space and technology. We bring together skills in programming, physics, research, design and storytelling, and we work as a team: we listen to every idea, share the workload fairly and learn from each other.
summary: Star Forge is a 16-bit educational game for students aged 12–17 that turns real space mission design into a hands-on challenge. Players choose a mission inspired by a real NASA mission (a CubeSat in low Earth orbit, the Pandora small satellite, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Perseverance and Artemis I), receive its launch vehicle and a limited budget, and split that budget across competing resources: structure, propulsion (delta-v), power, communications, science instruments and endurance. The twist: the minimum and optimal value of every resource is hidden. Players get only clues (distance to the destination, sunlight available, launch loads) and must reason like engineers, while keeping track of their own spending. Guided by AION, a robot assistant, they walk through a mission control room following JPL's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4), then watch the launch. If any resource falls below its minimum, the mission fails in a specific way and the game explains why. It matters because students rarely get to experience a full mission trade-off. Star Forge makes the core lesson of mission design tangible: improving one subsystem always costs something else. Every value is sourced from NASA and partner data, and the game is available in English and Spanish.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Star Forge is a desktop game (Python + Pygame) about the hardest part of mission design: balancing a limited budget across subsystems that compete with each other. It runs offline on macOS, Windows and Linux.

HOW IT WORKS
  1. Players create an avatar (body type, skin tone, hair, accessories and clothes are freely combinable and not labeled by gender) and choose a mission. Missions unlock in order: Easy (CubeSat to LEO, Electron), Normal (exoplanet small satellite, Falcon 9), Hard (Mars orbiter), Harder (Mars rover) and Insane (Moon orbiter, SLS Block 1). Each level adds one resource: from 2 resources in Easy to 6 in Insane.Mission grid: five missions inspired by real NASA missions, unlocked in order from Easy to Insane.
    1. CML 1 – Cocktail Napkin: confirm goal, destination and launch vehicle; the hangar doors open and reveal the rocket.
    2. CML 2 – Initial Feasibility: receive clues (e.g., Mars gets only 586 W/m² of sunlight, less than half of Earth's, per the NASA Mars Fact Sheet) stored in an archive.
    3. CML 3 – Trade Space: at one station per resource, type the amount (kg, m/s, W, Mbps, days) and see its cost. The total spent is never shown: players must track the budget themselves, and a robotic arm assembles each part in the hangar.
    4. CML 4 – Point Design: a budget review only says whether the design is over budget.The walkable mission control room (CML 3 – Trade Space) and the hangar where the rocket is assembled.
  2. The launch simulation follows a gravity turn and an orbit path. The first seconds are identical for success and failure; then the mission succeeds at its real destination or fails because of its weakest resource: the rocket breaks apart (structure), never reaches its target (delta-v), shuts down (power) or loses contact with Earth (communications).Launch simulation: the first seconds look the same whether the mission will succeed or fail.
  3. Results show each resource on a bar with zones (below minimum, acceptable, optimal, more than needed). Exact numbers are revealed only with 5 stars, so players learn by reasoning, not by copying. Try again returns to CML 4 with the previous values.Mission complete with 5 stars: only now are the exact minimum and optimal values revealed.A failed mission: each resource shows how close it was, without revealing the exact numbers.
THE SCIENCE

Propulsion uses the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation with real specific impulse and dry mass; solar power scales with the distance to the Sun; the Mars rover uses a nuclear power source like Perseverance. Optimal values are real mission values (e.g., MRO's 1,000 W solar arrays at Mars and 6 Mbps data rate, Orion's 11.2 kW European Service Module, Perseverance's 110 W MMRTG, Artemis I's 25.5-day duration). We audited every number against official sources and label team estimates as such. We validated every mission by searching hundreds of thousands of budget splits: each one has a 5-star solution, but guessing fails (no split in 10% steps completes Insane).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students practice systems thinking, estimation and real physics without formulas on screen, in English or Spanish. The difficulty grows gradually, the feedback explains why a mission failed, and the inclusive avatar helps every student see themselves as a mission designer.

TOOLS

Python 3, Pygame, JSON data files, GitHub. The game concept, mechanics, screen sketches, game design documents and mission data research were created by the team. AI tools (Claude, Claude Code) assisted in turning those sketches and documents into code, in verifying data against official sources, in validating the missions, and in translation and documentation. All pixel art, the pixel font and all sounds are generated procedurally by the game's code; no image, video or audio generation models were used. Mission preview images are NASA photos pixelated at runtime.
